confidence_note: The formula critique is the book's central argument. The 225-study / 275,000-person meta-analysis (Lyubomirsky, King & Diener 2005) is verified; its authors say the link runs both ways and much evidence is correlational. The doctors study (44 internists, small bag of candy) is from Achor's own account; Achor's 'nearly twice as fast' is kept as his claim. The Soweto scene comes from a chapter abstract (medium); the old '95 percent' is not used as a number.
facts: Achor questions the common formula: work hard, become successful, then be happy. Each success moves the goalpost, so happiness keeps being postponed.
His claim is the reverse order: happiness comes first and fuels performance.

A meta-analysis by Sonja Lyubomirsky, Laura King and Ed Diener reviewed 225 studies covering more than 275,000 people; happiness was linked to success at work, in relationships and in health, and often came before it. The authors say the influence runs both ways.
The meta-analysis also found happy people more inclined to seek out and take on new goals.

In one study, 44 doctors were asked to diagnose a patient from a file. Half were first given a small bag of candy as a thank-you, which they were not to eat during the task. The doctors in a good mood reached the correct diagnosis earlier; Achor puts it at nearly twice as fast.
Students who thought about the happiest day of their lives right before a maths test outperformed their peers.
Achor asked students at a school in Soweto who liked schoolwork; almost every hand went up. His escort said they saw schoolwork as a privilege their parents never had.
Achor's explanation: positive emotions flood the brain with dopamine and serotonin, which he says turn up the brain's learning centres, helping organise, keep and retrieve information faster.
scene_details: a bag of candy handed over and left unopened
a patient file being read toward a diagnosis
raised hands in a Soweto classroom
tension: A bag of candy no one ate changed how fast doctors found a diagnosis.
opening_idea: Start with the 44 doctors and the unopened bag of candy.

lessons.idea: Put a small good moment before hard work instead of saving it as the reward afterwards.
lessons.anchor: candy given before the diagnosis, not after

reflect_final: Which small pleasure do you only allow yourself after finishing a task, and what would change if you moved it to before you start?

use_cases.move: Mention the doctors who were given candy before the diagnosis; start with a minute of good news.

use_cases.situation: You've told yourself you'll relax once a project is done
use_cases.move: Move one small enjoyable thing to the start of the day.

use_cases.situation: A child must study for an exam
use_cases.move: Begin with a short happy memory or a laugh, then study.

pocket_idea: The doctors got their candy before the diagnosis; move your small reward to before the hard part.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Doctors given a bag of candy they didn't even eat found the right diagnosis faster.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Formula vs goalposts; meta-analysis 225 studies; 44 doctors candy; Achor's reverse order.
